title: AI's Wobbly House of Cards Is Now a Risk to Markets and the Economy
excerpt: Circular deals between OpenAI, Nvidia and Oracle have funded a $1 trillion AI buildout. Now credit markets are questioning who can actually pay for it.
body:
• Bloomberg's weekend analysis argues the AI boom's circular financing — vendors funding the customers that buy back their products — has made an AI correction a threat to the broader U.S. economy.
  • The deals are enormous: Nvidia's up-to-$100 billion investment in OpenAI, Oracle's $300 billion five-year OpenAI computing contract, and a fresh OpenAI chip pact with AMD — all struck within weeks of each other.
  • Credit markets are starting to flinch: about $18 billion of loans tied to an Oracle data center in New Mexico traded at 89 to 91 cents on the dollar this month after banks could not syndicate them to investors.
  • Hyperscalers have issued roughly $121 billion in new debt this year to fund AI initiatives — four times their five-year average — according to Bank of America.

The loop

Bloomberg's weekend verdict is blunt: the AI boom has become a wobbly house of cards, and the risk is no longer confined to technology stocks. At the center is the circular nature of the industry's financing. Nvidia agreed to invest as much as $100 billion in OpenAI to fund a massive data-center buildout; OpenAI, in turn, committed to filling those sites with millions of Nvidia chips. Nvidia is effectively funding OpenAI to buy Nvidia products.

OpenAI then ran the same play with AMD, agreeing to deploy tens of billions of dollars' worth of its chips, Bloomberg Law reported. The pattern extends across the ecosystem: Microsoft, which has put more than $13 billion into OpenAI, now accounts for nearly 20% of Nvidia's annual revenue, and Oracle's $300 billion, five-year OpenAI computing deal sits alongside a $100 million quarterly loss from renting data centers, mostly to OpenAI.

Context and background

The vendor-financing loop has an unhappy precedent. In the late 1990s, telecom vendors financed customers' equipment purchases and counted the spending as revenue — until it became clear there were few real end users paying real money.

"If all of a sudden there's a link in the chain that breaks, is counterparty X going to be able to pay counterparty Y?"

— Todd Castagno, analyst, in an interview with Sherwood

The scale of the commitments dwarfs anything the industry has attempted. OpenAI has committed roughly $1.4 trillion in future energy and compute procurement while expecting about $20 billion of revenue this year, according to industry analysis. Oracle, meanwhile, raised fiscal 2026 capital spending to a potential $50 billion-plus even as its long-term debt passed $99 billion and S&P cut its credit rating to one notch above junk in July.

What the credit market is saying

Until this year, Big Tech funded most AI spending from cash flow. Now leverage is doing more of the heavy lifting, and the credit market has noticed. About $18 billion in loans tied to Oracle's Project Jupiter data center in New Mexico — part of the $500 billion Stargate initiative led by OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle — are quoted at 89 to 91 cents on the dollar, the Financial Times reported on September 18. Syndicate banks including Santander and Jefferies have struggled to sell the debt amid concerns about Oracle's rising borrowing and weakening creditworthiness.

Separately, Nvidia has discussed guaranteeing as much as $250 billion in financing for an OpenAI data-center campus in Ohio — an exposure Reuters Breakingviews flagged as turning the chipmaker into a quasi-bank for AI infrastructure. Bank of America estimates hyperscalers have issued about $121 billion in new debt this year for AI, more than four times their $28 billion five-year average, with $96 billion in partner debt tied directly to OpenAI's build-out.

What's at stake for markets

The worry is not that AI is a fiction — even the critics grant the technology is real. It is that valuations, corporate balance sheets, and now bank credit have all been layered onto the same narrow bet: that OpenAI's revenue will scale fast enough to justify the commitments. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has dismissed extinction-level warnings as "doomsday narratives," but Bloomberg's point is systemic, not philosophical: the industry is so interconnected, and the capital so concentrated, that a stumble at the top of the chain now reaches the economy itself — through equity, credit, and recession channels.

What's next

Three signals to watch. First, Anthropic's delayed IPO — now expected about a month later than planned — may reprice the private AI valuations underpinning this financing. Second, whether Oracle's debt markets stabilize or keep discounting AI infrastructure loans, the first real price signal on AI credit risk. And third, hyperscaler earnings: capex guidance and commentary on returns will show whether the spending is buying productivity or just buying time. For portfolio investors, the lesson is concrete: check how much of your equity and bond exposure is ultimately a bet on one customer's ability to keep spending.
image_caption: The New York Stock Exchange. Analysts warn the AI trade's wobbly valuations are becoming a risk to markets and the broader economy.
nri_angle: For Indian and diaspora investors with heavy exposure to U.S. tech stocks, index funds and Big Tech debt, the AI financing chain is now a portfolio-level risk, not just a tech story.
